summary: Provides a list of terms used in the IETF when discussing internationalization, to help frame discussions and introduce key concepts to participants. It is a best current practice.

plainLanguage.summary: This document is a shared list of words for talking about text in different languages. It exists so that people in different IETF working groups use the same words for the same ideas when they discuss whether a protocol should carry text other than plain English letters.

questions: what is internationalization in the ietf

subtitle: A shared glossary so IETF working groups mean the same thing when they talk about languages, scripts, characters and encodings.

tldr.problem: IETF working groups often have no internationalization expert, so discussions about text in different languages drift into different vocabulary and different assumptions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC is a glossary that defines the terms used when the IETF discusses internationalization, drawing on ISO/IEC 10646, the Unicode Standard, the W3C Character Model and earlier IETF documents.
tldr.outcome: Its definitions SHOULD be used by IETF standards unless a standard provides a different definition for a term. It is a Best Current Practice and it obsoletes RFC 3536.

facts.value: The first 2^16 code points, also called Plane 0

facts.value: 1 to 3 octets in the BMP, 4 octets outside it

today: RFC 6365 is an Internet Best Current Practice, BCP 166, published in September 2011. It obsoleted RFC 3536 and has not been obsoleted since. The document defines vocabulary rather than a protocol, so it is read as a reference rather than implemented.

sections.title: Purpose and How to Read the Definitions
sections.content:
The Character Set Policy specification RFC 2277 summarises the problem in a single line: internationalization is for humans, which means that protocols are not subject to internationalization, text strings are. Many IETF protocols carry text strings that people enter or read, so it should be possible for anyone to enter or read those strings, in any human language, using typical input methods.

This document is a glossary of the terms the IETF uses when it discusses internationalization. Its purpose is to frame discussions in the many working groups where the subject comes up, and to introduce the main concepts to participants. Few of those groups have internationalization experts, so the recurring question of whether a protocol has to be internationalized needs a shared answer.

The definitions here SHOULD be used by IETF standards. A standard that wants a different definition for one of these terms can provide one, but unless it does, the definitions in this document apply. Standards that need a different definition are encouraged, for clarity, to use different words instead. The main sources are ISO/IEC 10646, the Unicode Standard, the W3C Character Model, and IETF documents including RFC 2277 and RFC 5890.

The source of each definition is shown in angle brackets in the body of the document, and definitions written for this document are marked with the tag RFC6365. Text after the angle brackets is commentary, not part of the definition. Appendix C lists the significant changes from RFC 3536, which this document obsoletes: the status became a Best Current Practice, terms used in IDNA2008 were added, the term 'variant' is now discussed in some detail, a section on subsets of the Unicode repertoire was added, and a new term, 'writing style', was introduced.
sections.plainLanguage: This document collects the words the IETF uses when it talks about text in other languages, so that different working groups argue from the same definitions. The definitions are meant to be used by other standards unless those standards say otherwise.

sections.title: Fundamental Terms
sections.content:
A language is a way that humans communicate, in speech, writing or signing; computer languages are explicitly excluded. A script is a set of graphic characters used for the written form of one or more languages, such as Latin, Cyrillic, Greek, Arabic and Han. A writing system is a set of rules for using one or more scripts to write a particular language, such as the American English or the Japanese writing system. Novices often mix up language and script, and that matters in protocols that treat the two differently: almost all protocols that handle non-ASCII text deal with scripts or characters, and fewer deal with languages.

The names do not line up one to one. A single name can mean either a language or a script, as 'Arabic' does. Many scripts are used to write more than one language, as Cyrillic is used for Russian and Bulgarian. Some languages are written in more than one script at the same time, as Japanese is written in the Kanji, Katakana and Hiragana scripts in a single string of text.

A character is a member of a set of elements used for the organisation, control or representation of data. A particular character is identified by its name, not by its shape: a name may suggest a meaning, but the character may be used for other meanings too. A coded character set (CCS) is a set of unambiguous rules that establishes a character set and the relationship between its characters and their coded representation. The collection of characters in a character set is its repertoire. A character encoding form maps a coded character set to the code units used to represent the data, and a character encoding scheme is an encoding form plus byte serialization, which is why there are many character encoding schemes in Unicode, such as UTF-8 and UTF-16BE. A charset is in effect a combination of one or more coded character sets with a character encoding scheme, and charset names are registered by IANA. The RFC prefers the terms 'charset', 'character encoding scheme' and 'coded character set' over 'character set', because 'character set' has other meanings outside the IETF.

A glyph is an image of a character that can be displayed after being imaged onto a display surface, and a glyph code is a numeric code that refers to a glyph within a font. Transcoding converts text data from one character encoding form to another, and works only at the level of encoding, without parsing the text.

In the IETF, internationalization means adding or improving the handling of non-ASCII text in a protocol. Localization is adapting an internationalized application to a specific cultural environment, keeping the semantics and changing the syntax, and it is rarely an IETF matter: protocols that are merely localized, even serially for several locations, are generally considered unsatisfactory for the global Internet. The abbreviations i18n and l10n stand for internationalization and localization, counting the characters between the first and last letter. The term 'multilingual' has so many varying definitions that the RFC says it should not be used in standards.
sections.plainLanguage: The document separates several words that are often confused. A language is what people speak or write, a script is the set of characters used to write it, and a character is one member of that set. It also separates the set of characters from the byte encoding that carries them.

sections.title: Standards Bodies, Encodings and Charsets
sections.content:
Three groups matter most. ISO and ISO/IEC JTC 1 have worked on character standards since before the IETF existed, and their standard used most in the IETF is ISO/IEC 10646, a coded character set that covers almost all known written characters in use today; it is controlled by SC2/WG2. ISO 639 gives the names of languages and forms the basis of the IETF's Language Tag work, and ISO 3166 gives the names and codes for countries and territories. The Unicode Consortium maintains the Unicode Standard, which is a coded character set whose repertoire and code points are identical to ISO/IEC 10646, and adds character attributes such as case conversion and numeric properties that are not part of ISO/IEC 10646. A reciprocal agreement between the two bodies keeps their definitions of characters and code points in step, and the IETF's preference has shifted from citing ISO/IEC 10646 to citing Unicode because of those attributes and because the Unicode specifications are freely available. The W3C created and maintains XML, which has always been fully internationalized.

Characters in ISO/IEC 10646 can be expressed in many ways. The Basic Multilingual Plane (BMP) is the first 2^16 code points and contains almost all characters in contemporary use; it is also called Plane 0. UCS-2 addresses only the BMP, and because many useful characters such as many Han characters are defined outside it, many people consider UCS-2 obsolete. UCS-4 addresses the entire range of code points, 0 to 0x10FFFF, as 32-bit values with zero padding on the left, and is identical to UTF-32BE without a byte order mark.

UTF-8 is the preferred encoding for IETF protocols. Characters in the BMP are encoded as one, two or three octets, and characters outside the BMP as four octets; characters from the US-ASCII repertoire have the same on-the-wire representation in UTF-8 as in US-ASCII. UTF-16, UTF-16BE and UTF-16LE are required by no IETF standard and are therefore used far less often; characters in the BMP are always two octets, and characters outside it are four octets using a surrogate pair. UTF-16 and UTF-32 differ in the byte order and in the presence or absence of a byte order mark. SCSU and BOCU-1 are Unicode encodings designed for compression, and although compression is attractive, neither has attracted much interest.

Many countries also developed their own coded character sets before ISO/IEC 10646 existed, and many dozen are in common use on the Internet, such as ISO 8859-5 for Cyrillic and Shift-JIS for Japanese. The official list of registered charset names is maintained by IANA, and that list has historically contained many errors. ASCII is the most widely known native coded character set and is the basis for keywords and parameter names in many IETF protocols; strictly speaking ASCII is a coded character set and repertoire, not an encoding, and the encoding used for ASCII in IETF protocols is the 7-bit integer code point right-justified in an 8-bit field, sometimes called the Network Virtual Terminal encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Two standards define almost all the characters in use: ISO/IEC 10646 and the Unicode Standard, which agree on the same repertoire and code points. The RFC recommends UTF-8 for protocols, because ASCII text keeps the same bytes and every other character fits in at most four octets.

sections.title: Combining Characters, Normalization, Case and Collation
sections.content:
A code point is a value in the codespace of a repertoire. A combining character is a member of an identified subset of the coded character set intended for combination with the preceding non-combining graphic character, and combining characters are inherently non-spacing. A composite sequence is a non-combining character followed by one or more combining characters; it is not a character, and therefore not a member of the repertoire of ISO/IEC 10646. The same letter can exist in a coded character set as a single code point or as a combination of several characters. The rules for combining characters are called composition rules and the rules for taking a character apart are decomposition rules; the result of decomposition is a decomposed character and the result of composition is usually a precomposed character.

Normalization is the transformation of data to a normal form. Here 'unify spelling' means unifying different character sequences intended to form the same composite characters, not unifying different words with the same meaning. Its purpose is to allow two strings to be compared for equivalence: the strings that spell a word with a precomposed tilde and with a combining tilde look identical on screen, and a protocol that wants them to count as equal must say where normalization happens. The Unicode NFC and NFD normalizations support canonical equivalence, and NFKC and NFKD support canonical and compatibility equivalence.

Case is the feature of certain alphabets where letters have two or occasionally more distinct forms, the uppercase and the lowercase. Case mapping associates the two forms. There is usually, but not always, a one-to-one mapping between the two cases of a letter: the Turkish dotless 'i', some Greek characters with modifiers, and the German Sharp S and Greek final sigma have no straightforward counterpart, and case mapping can even depend on locale or language. Converting text to a single case for comparison is called case folding, and the RFC notes that some case folding algorithms, such as those in Java, are locale-sensitive and therefore resource-intensive and behave differently depending on where the system is.

Collation is the process of ordering units of textual information, usually specific to a language, an application or a locale. Collation works out the relative order of pairs of strings, and the orders can differ widely: even within ASCII characters, 'A, a, B, b' and 'A, B, C, ..., Z, a, b' are both common and very different orders. Sorting is the process of putting data records into specified orders. For only a few character set and encoding combinations is the code point order the obvious sort order; for many others it makes no sense to a person, and sorting to code point order also looks inconsistent when the strings are not normalized first, because different representations of the same character sort differently.
sections.plainLanguage: The same visible letter can be stored in more than one way, so the RFC explains how to turn text into a standard form before comparing it. It also covers uppercase and lowercase, and the fact that the right order for strings depends on the language rather than on the character codes.

sections.title: Types of Characters and Subsets
sections.content:
The RFC collects the character types that application designers need to think about, and warns that the definitions do not cleanly put every character in exactly one type. Alphabetic characters are the primary units of alphabets and syllabaries, whether combining or not. Ideographic characters primarily denote an idea rather than a sound, such as the Han characters used in Chinese, Japanese and Korean, although the convention describes the script as ideographic as contrasted to alphabetic. Numbers are distinguished by Unicode with a special general category, subdivided into decimal digits, letter digits and other digits. Punctuation characters separate units of text such as sentences and phrases, and are also used in mathematical and scientific formulae. Symbols are characters other than letters, digits or punctuation, covering mathematical operators, optical character recognition symbols, box-drawing characters, dingbats, arrows, faces and geometric shapes.

A nonspacing character is a combining character whose position depends on its base character and which does not itself consume space along the visual baseline; a combining acute accent, U+0301, is an example. A diacritic is a mark applied to a symbol to create a new symbol representing a modified or new value, or a mark applied regardless of whether it changes the value, in which case it usually carries independent linguistic information such as an accent or tone. Control characters are the 65 characters in the ranges U+0000 to U+001F and U+007F to U+009F; the basic space, U+0020, is often counted as one too, making 66. They are also known as control codes, and the terminology treats them as three ranges: C0 for U+0000 to U+001F, C1 for U+0080 to U+009F, and the single control character DEL at U+007F. Formatting characters are inherently invisible but affect the surrounding characters, for example by specifying the direction of text or how to join characters. A compatibility character is a graphic character included mainly for compatibility with existing coded character sets, such as the fullwidth exclamation mark U+FF01, which exists for compatibility with Asian charsets that include full-width and half-width ASCII characters.

Subsets of characters need care. Older coded character sets such as ASCII and the ISO 8859 family are close-ended and fixed, while Unicode is open-ended, with new characters and often new scripts added every year or so. A subset such as 'uppercase letters' can be given as a range of code points in ASCII, but a similar definition for Unicode either has to be expressed in terms of Unicode properties or depends on the Unicode version, and the version must then be identified in the specification.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the kinds of character a protocol may carry: letters, symbols, punctuation, marks that decorate a letter, invisible formatting instructions and control codes. It also warns that Unicode keeps growing, so a rule that names a set of characters has to say which version it applies to.

sections.title: Entering, Displaying and Carrying Text
sections.content:
Although the IETF does not standardize user interfaces, many protocols make assumptions about how a user will enter or see text. An input method is a mechanism for a person to enter text into an application. Many characters cannot be typed on a typical keyboard in a single stroke, and operating systems provide software that lets users enter characters outside the keyboard range; there are dozens of input methods for Han characters in Chinese, Japanese and Korean, some based on phonetic input and some on the number of strokes. The term 'input method editor', IME, is used for the tools that handle this.

A rendering rule is an algorithm a system uses to decide how to display a string of text. Some scripts can be displayed directly from fonts, but others need rules based on the surrounding characters. Arabic changes the form of a letter depending on whether it stands alone or begins, continues or ends a word. Indic scripts may change a consonant's form next to certain other consonants, or display characters in an order different from the order they are stored in. Arabic and Hebrew reorder characters according to the bidirectional properties of the characters and the right-to-left and left-to-right ordering marks. Many systems substitute a small open box or a question mark when they lack a font for a character. A font is a collection of glyphs used for the visual depiction of character data, and is often associated with parameters such as size, posture, weight and serifness; 'typeface' usually means a family of fonts sharing a general design, such as Times Roman with its Bold, Medium and Italic variants.

Bidirectional display is the mixing of left-to-right and right-to-left text in a single line, often abbreviated 'bidi'. Most written languages are displayed left to right, but many widely used ones, based on Hebrew or Arabic, are displayed primarily right to left. Right-to-left text confuses protocol writers because they must keep thinking in terms of the order of characters in a string, which may differ from what appears on screen. A undisplayable character is one with no displayable form, such as the zero-width space U+200B and the formatting characters that set text direction. A writing style is a convention for writing the same script in a different style: Perso-Arabic Nastalique and Arabic Naskh both use the Arabic script but have very different renderings and are not mutually comprehensible, and Nastalique needs significantly more line height.

In protocols, a protocol element is a uniquely named part of a protocol, such as 'source port' in TCP. Where the names are transmitted, as the verb names are in SMTP, they are part of the protocol standard; they are rarely seen by end users and it is rarely appropriate to internationalize them, even when the elements themselves are internationalized. A name space is the set of valid names for an item, or the rules for generating them; names may be generated, registered centrally with IANA, or registered in a distributed way as DNS names are. The on-the-wire encoding is the encoding and decoding used before and after transmission; characters are identified by code points, must be encoded as bits and octets before transmission, and must be decoded before a protocol can process them individually.

Parsed text is text that has been analysed for its parts. Mail user agents often parse the Subject header to thread conversations by what follows the 'Re:' prefix, and such conventions are sensitive to localization: if a mail user agent rewrites 'Re:' to match the sender's language, a system that later threads on it may not recognise the replacement. Charset identification names the charset used for a string of text, and language identification names the human language used in it, which is also called language tagging; the Language Tag standards RFC 5646 and RFC 4647 provide the model for language identification.

MIME is a message format that allows textual message bodies and headers in character sets other than US-ASCII, in formats that require ASCII, and is described in RFCs 2045 through 2049. A transfer encoding syntax is a reversible transform of already encoded data, used mainly to carry new types of data over legacy protocols; the main examples in the IETF are Base64 and quoted-printable. Base64 represents binary data using the ASCII characters A to Z, a to z, 0 to 9, plus, slash and equals sign. Quoted-printable lets strings with non-ASCII characters mixed into mostly ASCII printable text stay somewhat human readable, although the RFC calls it a failure at being readable and notes that it is jokingly called 'quoted unreadable'. XML text that is not encoded as UTF-8 is explicitly tagged with charsets, and all XML text consists only of Unicode characters. ASN.1 text formats include IA5String, PrintableString, BMPString, UTF8String and TeletexString, each allowing a different repertoire and encoding.
sections.plainLanguage: Two things decide whether a protocol handles text well: how a person enters it, and how the bytes travel. The RFC covers input methods, the rules a display engine follows for Arabic and Indic scripts, and the labels a protocol needs so a receiver knows which encoding and which language it has.

sections.title: Domain Names, Variants and Other Common Terms
sections.content:
The current specification for Internationalized Domain Names (IDNs), known formally as Internationalized Domain Names for Applications or IDNA, is referred to as 'IDNA2008' and consists of several documents. RFC 5890 provides the definitions and introduces specialised terms for the different kinds of DNS label in an IDN context: the ACE Prefix, the A-label, the Domain Name Slot, the IDNA-valid string, the Internationalized Domain Name and Label, the LDH Label, the Non-Reserved LDH label and the U-label. Two more terms came from the earlier effort. Stringprep provides a model and character tables for preparing internationalized strings; it was used in the original specification, IDNA2003, through a profile called Nameprep, and is no longer in use in IDNA but continues to be used by other protocols. Punycode is the name of the algorithm that converts otherwise-valid IDN labels from native-character strings in Unicode to an ASCII-compatible encoding; strictly speaking the term applies to the algorithm only, though in practice it is widely used for the strings it produces.

The term variant entered the IETF's internationalization vocabulary with the JET recommendations, where it referred strictly to the relationship between Traditional Chinese characters and their Simplified equivalents. It has since been used more widely for collections of characters or strings that might be perceived as equivalent: visually similar or confusable characters, such as ASCII 'l' and '1' or Latin and Cyrillic 'a'; characters assigned more than one code point, such as the Arabic YEH or the Greek final sigma; numerals and labels including them, since the Arabic script has two sets of digits that differ for four through six; and orthographic differences within a language, such as 'color' and 'colour' in English. The RFC warns that the term should not be confused with other uses, and that context should distinguish variant characters from variant labels.

Section 8 collects further terms used in the same discussions. Locale is the user-specific location and cultural information managed by a computer, typically including the language or languages used, and often extending to the display format for currency, dates and times; some locales, including the popular 'C' and 'POSIX' locales, carry no language information. The RFC notes that many thorny, unsolved issues remain with locale, such as whether text should be viewed using the locale of the person who wrote it, of the system storing it, or of the person viewing it.

Romanization is the transliteration of a non-Latin script into Latin characters; there are two popular romanizations of Chinese, Wade-Giles and Pinyin, the latter far more common today, and many romanization systems are inexact and do not round-trip. Translation conveys the meaning of a passage from one language so that it can be expressed equivalently in another; many translation systems are inexact and cannot be applied repeatedly. Transliteration represents the characters of an alphabetical or syllabic writing system with the characters of a conversion alphabet, generally letter by letter, and many transliterations are exact and round-trip cleanly. Transcription systematically writes the sounds of spoken language, usually with a technical phonetic alphabet, and unlike transliterations is almost never round-trip convertible. Regular expressions select specific strings from a set of character strings, and there is no single regular expression language but numerous similar dialects that are not quite consistent with each other.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC ends with the vocabulary used for internationalized domain names, such as Punycode and the labels IDNA defines, and with words for words that look or sound alike. It warns that 'variant' covers several different ideas, so a protocol using the word has to say which one it means.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says plainly that security is not discussed directly in the document. The definitions it gives have no direct effect on security, but they are used in many security contexts: authentication usually involves comparing two tokens, and one or both of those tokens might be text, so some methods of comparison involve the internationalization concepts defined here.

Other RFCs dealing with internationalization do have security consideration descriptions that may be useful to the reader. In particular, the security considerations in RFC 3454, RFC 3629, RFC 4013 and RFC 5890 go into a fair amount of detail.
sections.plainLanguage: This document defines words rather than behaviour, so it sets no security rules of its own. It points to four other RFCs that do discuss security for text handling.
